speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Will the minister give the house an up to date report in respect to the alleged violations of the cease fire in Laos?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO VIOLATIONS OF CEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the commission returned to Laos it has received a number of complaints about breaches of the cease fire. These complaints have been from both sides. They have been considered and discussed with the leaders of the principal parties.
The commission has received assurances that no intentional violation of the cease fire had taken place and that whatever actions had occurred had been taken under provocation and in exercise of the right of self defence.
The hon. member for Trinity will realize that absolute control over widely scattered forces is difficult because of the absence of a detailed cease fire agreement, the nature of the terrain, which of course is exceedingly difficult, and the lack of communication between commands. Nevertheless the commission has decided to send representatives to two areas, one in the north and one in the south, where the most serious incidents are reported to have taken place. The intention of the commission to carry out these investigations was communicated to the leaders of the various parties in Laos on May 22; that is, four days ago. As yet I have no information on the results of the investigations.
I might say in addition that, as the hon. member will recall, at our urging in Geneva the co-chairmen, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union, wired the chairman of the international commission for a submission as to what equipment that commission would need. The reply has now been received and it goes into some detail in connection with the requirements of the commission. If these 90205-6-341J
requirements are met by the co-chairmen the work of the commission will be greatly facilitated.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO CAUSE OF DEATH OF FISH
speechtext:
On
May 19 the hon. member for Kootenay West directed a question to the Minister of Fisheries as follows:
In view of reports that dead codfish and herring have been noted floating in Newfoundland's Fortune bay and in other waters off the western shore, which is puzzling even the most experienced and oldest fishermen of that island province, would the minister inform the house whether he is having this situation investigated in an attempt to

discover what is causing the death of these fish and, particularly, whether radioactive wastes are a factor.
In the absence of the Minister of Fisheries, I should like to reply. This matter was thoroughly investigated by officials of the Department of Fisheries in Newfoundland, including Dr. Templeman, director of the biological station of the fisheries research board at St. John's. These officials report that the story in the press was exaggerated. The incident occurred during January or February of this year, and I am advised that it could have been caused by codfish pursuing herring bait and suddenly entering extremely cold water near the surface. The abrupt change in water temperature could easily cause mortality among the fish. The officials in Newfoundland also report it is extremely doubtful that the cause was radioactive waste. There is no evidence that large quantities of dead fish were involved.
I hope the hon. member will not think I am being unduly frivolous if I add that the poor fish are unlike human beings inasmuch as they get into trouble when they get into cold water.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: SAINT JOHN, N.B.    REPORTED PROVISION OF BEDS TO IMMIGRANT STRIKEBREAKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Skeena asked whether there was any truth in the allegation that immigration officers in Saint John, New Brunswick, were suppling beds and bedding to immigrant strikebreakers at the Saint John Dry dock Company, whose employees have been on strike for the past four or five weeks.
The first complaint I received in the matter of this strike was from the industrial union of marine and shipbuilding workers of Canada in Saint John. It was alleged that the Saint John Drydock Company intended to import labour from abroad to replace Canadian workers on strike. For some time prior to the strike this company had been recruiting, with the assistance of my officials abroad, specialized workers in the United Kingdom. They had been unable to recruit these workers anywhere in Canada, even with the assistance of the national employment service. To the best of my knowledge only a few men came to Canada before the strike began. Since the strike immigration officials in the United Kingdom have been holding in abeyance applications received from prospective immigrants coming forward to the Saint John
[Mr. Herridge.l
Drydock Company until confirmation is received that the company is no longer strike bound.
The second complaint was from the general strike committee in Saint John. It was alleged that the local immigration office was assisting the company by recruiting strikebreakers from newly arrived immigrants and was supplying them with beds and bedding at a private home in Saint John. An investigation has clearly established that there is no basis whatever for this complaint. The owner of the private home which was mentioned in the complaint is not even known to our officers, and no immigrant has been referred for employment to the Saint John Drydock Company since the strike began. It has been suggested to the general strike committee that these matters could best be clarified and settled by direct liaison between the committee in Saint John and the local immigration office.

Mr. Chairman, examining the estimates submitted by the Department of Justice and comparing them with the main and supplementary estimates submitted for the previous fiscal year, or comparing them with those for 1959-60, I find certain discrepancies.
That is why I should like to put a few questions to the Minister of Justice.
If one takes the blue book tabled this year, which indicates that this year the same method was followed as in every other year, one sees in the first column the amounts we are asked to vote for the current fiscal year; the second column shows the amounts voted by the house for the previous fiscal, that is the 1960-61 fiscal year.
That second column is made up of the main and supplementary estimates we voted. In addition, we have the supplementary estimates which were introduced only after the blue book was printed and distributed, I think, around February.
This year the same procedure was followed as in previous years, that is in 1960-61 and in 1959-60.
Having indicated, Mr. Chairman, what I believe to be the truth concerning the procedure to be followed and that which was followed, I should like now to make a few remarks based on figures taken from the estimates, and with your permission I shall begin with the fiscal year 1959-60. These figures include items to be discussed as well as statutory votes.
According to page 34 of the blue book for the fiscal year 1959-60, we voted an amount of $27,335,204 in the main estimates.

Later during the year we were asked to vote supplementary estimates. At this point I refer the committee to page 4 of the supplementary estimates. We had voted an amount of $1,727,541.
These amounts together give a total of $29,062,745.
We also voted other supplementary estimates included in the new supplementary estimates No. 2. The amount was $52,300, which gives a grand total of $29,115,045 for the year 1959-60.
And now, I want to refer to the blue book for the 1960-61 fiscal year and to the second column which includes main and supplementary estimates for the previous year; I find a total of $29,062,745, which is the amount we voted then in main and supplementary estimates. This means that at the time the blue book for the 1960-61 fiscal year was printed, supplementary estimates No. 2 were not included.
Now, if I take the amounts we voted last year and that we find in the first column of the 1960-61 blue book, I find-at page 34 of that book-that the total amount of the main estimates is $26,382,901. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a very few remarks in connection with the bill of rights, because I have heard it mentioned both in the house and outside. This act, in the very brief time since last summer during which it has been in effect, has been frequently invoked and fulfils a notable function in our system of jurisprudence. I think a grave disservice is being done by those who seek to scoff at its usefulness by attempting to attribute to this law certain characteristics which were not and could not be attached to it, and then saying that the bill has failed in its purpose because in these respects it did not serve to protect certain individuals.
In the first instance, many of the cases where it has been suggested there has been a failure on the part of the bill of rights have been concerned with matters entirely within provincial jurisdiction. Time after time I have heard statements pointing out certain alleged weaknesses in this legislation with reference to injustices which it has created. In many of these cases there is no doubt that provincial laws and regulations were involved. It is my respectful submission that if much of the energy which is misdirected in improperly attacking and criticizing the bill of rights was instead used in trying to persuade provincial 90205-6-342
Supply-Justice
legislatures to pass complementary legislation, that is provincial bills of rights, which will have the same effect in the provincial field that this bill of rights has in the federal field, it would be a very fine thing.
In many cases there has been an erroneous conception of the way to make use of the law. Not only is it a shield against oppression; it is also a sword with which to obtain rights. But it is a sword that must be properly used. In many instances the person to use it is the individual whose rights have been curtailed or interfered with.
Thus if a person is removed from his employment because of his employer relying upon a clause or provision in the contract of employment, and the employee thinks the dismissal contravenes the bill of rights, one remedy is an action for damages for wrongful dismissal. This may not give the same measure of publicity for those in public life who seek publicity, and it may not make an interesting news story for those who write about it, but what is most important is that it does ensure some measure of reparation for those who are entitled to it.
I would ask the minister, before the estimates of his department are completed, to give the committee any statistical information he may have as to the number of instances in which the bill of rights has been invoked. I know that in due course there will be a body of jurisprudence built up and established in the law reports of the country. However, I am wondering whether at this time the minister or his officials have been able to secure any information as to the number of instances in which people have invoked the bill of rights in connection with certain matters before the courts.
I have read a great many news stories, as I am sure other hon. members have. If you take those as being that part of the iceberg which is above water, there is no question at all that this legislation, in the very brief time since it was passed, has been of great value and service. As a practising lawyer over many years I know there are instances which I look back upon where the presence of this legislation would have served to secure redress for my clients.
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Chairman, there are two other matters I should like to place before the minister under this item by way of suggestion. First there is the question of the procedure for dealing with appeals from magisterial convictions. I think the hon. member for Welland said the other day that before the magistrates' courts is where you find the greatest percentage of people who make their first contact with the administration of justice, and the right of appeal from

Supply-Justice
magistrates' courts should be carefully guarded. It has been my experience, and it has been brought to my attention, that sometimes difficulties and impediments do arise under section 722 of the Criminal Code, which is the section dealing with the procedure as to service of notice of appeal, because it is not possible to seek out and serve the respondent or the informant within the time limit provided by that section. Sometimes it is not possible to serve the person who was the informant and would be the respondent. This is particularly true in the more remote areas of the country and, I think, in many rural districts.
I would ask the minister to give some consideration to introducing an amendment to the code by which provision for substituted service could be provided. In addition I would ask the minister to give consideration to extending the time within which the notice should be served and the proper affidavits filed either before or after the expiration of the 30 day limit. In my experience this would be very useful and would give appellants the right to which they are entitled which sometimes, because of the present rigid requirement of the law, is not the case. This is a statutory right of appeal, and all judges insist that there be rigid compliance with all the requirements.
The other question I should like to ask the minister at this time is whether he would give consideration or has given consideration to amending the present law in the Criminal Code where penalties and offences are set out in so far as driving automobiles is concerned. The minister will recall that a number of years ago we had what was known as the offence of dangerous driving. As I now read the code we are limited at the present time to the offence of criminal negligence. It has been my experience, and this experience is reinforced by statements which have been made to me by people who should know, that it is becoming increasingly difficult to secure a conviction on a charge of criminal negligence.
Having in mind the slaughter and the necessity of striving to cut down the accidents and this dreadful toll of human lives which continues to infest our highways, does the minister think it might be worth while to consider restoring an offence of an intermediate nature where convictions might more readily be obtained, rather than having only the offence of criminal negligence, of which juries and judges are loath to convict?

Mr. Chairman, I want to take advantage of this item to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee a certain 
circumstance that affected a young lady, which clearly demonstrates the ineffectiveness of the present bill of rights to protect the freedoms of Canadians. I support the principle of the bill, but I am rising briefly to bring this to the attention of the minister to indicate that we must go further. We have either to incorporate the bill in the constitution or get agreement with the provinces to enact enabling legislation.
In the Calgary Albertan of May 11 this year I read an article entitled "Free speech? Fire girl for talk". The article continues:
Miss Valerie Smith, the young Calgary draftsman who spoke a kind word for Cuba under Castro at Tuesday's meeting of the Knights of the Round Table, has been fired from her job. Miss Smith, an employee of Midwest Surveys Ltd. for the past 3J years, was dismissed Wednesday morning by the company's manager, J. J. Simpson, after an account of her speech at the Knights of the Round Table appeared in The Albertan.
I have a copy of the speech here which I have read with interest, and hon. members may wish to know that the factual information contained in it is based on a report by Professor Samuel Shapiro, assistant professor of history at Michigan State University (Oakland) and also on various articles which appeared in The Nation which as we all know, is a United States magazine.
I think this raises an important question, and the reaction to this young lady's dismissal shows the extent of the public interest in the preservation of fundamental rights and human freedoms for Canadian citizens. No one with an objective turn of mind, reading this speech, could see any reason for this young lady suffering dismissal for expressing her views. Some people might not agree with those views, but they are presented in a fair and clear manner. The public interest to which I have referred was indicated by the Knights of the Round Table themselves, who have written letters to various members of this house. Here is one of these letters, addressed to the hon. member for Assiniboia:
We, the undersigned, were all present at the meeting of the Calgary Knights of the Round Table on Tuesday, May 9, when Miss Valerie Smith spoke on Cuba.
Speaking only as individuals, and not officially for the Table, we wish to state our opinion that Miss Smith's report on what she saw in Cuba was very similar to those of other unprejudiced observers, dealing, as it did, chiefly with the improved living conditions of the rural population and better educational opportunities generally.
I have had Canadian Press men tell me that within the last two or three weeks.
The Knights of the Round Table is an organization of business and professional men and has been in existence for some 35 years. It prides

itself on offering a platform for the free expression of opinion on any question however controversial. Consequently we feel very concerned at the unjust treatment of Miss Smith by her employer.
This letter is signed by half a dozen members of the Calgary branch of the Knights of the Round Table. I noticed, in addition, a press item which appeared on May 12 in the Albertan, as follows:
The Knights of the Round Table, a group of leading Calgary business and professional men, Thursday night "deplored" the firing of Miss Valerie Smith for expressing pro-Cuban and pro-Castro sentiments.
Miss Smith, who addressed the Round Table on her return from Cuba, was fired from her drafting job with Midwest Surveys Ltd.
In a statement to the Albertan, Charles S. Lee, president of the Knights of the Round Table said "We are a forum for free expression where all shades of opinion may be presented."
That is the very basis of democracy:
"The existence of freedom of speech in the community is put to the test when someone expresses an unpopular view.
"Any action to penalize a speaker or deprive him or her of natural and legitimate rights is deplored by this Table, and we are anxious that any action of this kind should not pass without protest".
Then again, I notice that the Alberta federation of labour has shown an interest in this case, as is clear from the following report which also appeared in the Albertan on May 16:
The Alberta federation of labour will request the provincial government to immediately enact a fair employment practices act, Frank Bodie, A.F.L. executive secretary, announced Monday.
The move of labour was sparked by the dismissal of Miss Valerie Smith following her recent talk to the Knights of the Round Table in which she praised conditions as she saw them in Castro's Cuba on a two week holiday.
The A.F.L. will also protest the company's action in a letter to the board of industrial relations.
In addition to the numerous articles and letters which have appeared in the Alberta newspapers, we have received a good number of letters ourselves. I have one in my hand, Mr. Chairman, asking that some of us should raise the question in the house since it is felt to be a supreme example of discrimination but which has far wider implications-these are the words of my correspondent-in that it will result in the muzzling of any citizen who does not choose to be subservient to the generally accepted opinions. This letter goes on to ask that the question be brought before the Minister of Justice in order that he may consider whether it would be possible to amend the bill of rights so as to make it more effective, or to incorporate the bill of rights in our constitution.
I fully appreciate the difficulties in this regard because of the nature of our constitution, but I do think a case such as this 90205-6-342i
Supply-Justice
demonstrates clearly the necessity for the government to continue to press for the incorporation of the bill of rights into the constitution or for the co-operation of the provinces in passing enabling legislation to support it.
The dismissal of this girl was, possibly, an action taken in haste because the manager in question was irritated by the views she had expressed. As I said before, in my opinion the speech was very tolerant and moderate in tone. It expressed the view that Castro is doing a great deal for the Cuban people, and so on, but that is a matter of opinion. Good gracious; if we do not allow an individual to express unpopular opinions, democracy cannot survive. We need to take an example from Great Britain, where you can go any day of the week, particularly to Hyde park, and hear people talking about the desirability of burning down Buckingham Palace; and there is a constable on duty nearby to protect them while they say it.
I shall never forget being in Britain during the Suez crisis. I was in the House of Lords on the second day of the debate. The universities sent delegations to London to protest the action being taken by the government. They came in busloads from Oxford, from Bristol, from Manchester and from other towns all over Britain. They paraded in front of the palace of Westminster. We were provided with a stand in front of the building by an official of the commonwealth parliamentary association and we saw them as they went by holding up banners containing such slogans as "Down with Eden", "Stop the Murders", and all the rest of it. Policemen were walking alongside. Then following were thousands of members of the communist party carrying the union jack and the red flag, marching in columns. Those in the crowd, instead of hurling bottles and invectives behaved in an altogether different manner. I heard one old cockney standing to my right shouting as the red flag went by "Blimey, mate, where did you get that bloody old rag from?"
That is the spirit which preserves democracy; that is the spirit in which fair play is maintained, and in these circumstances people rally to the defence of democracy. People who become irritated and are impelled to all kinds of hasty action when opinions are expressed with which they do not agree, do not understand what democracy really means.
As I say, I undertook to bring this question to the attention of the minister and I should like him, later on, to refer to the incident in question and inform the committee what is being done at the present time to secure a wider acceptance of the bill of rights

Supply-Justice
and ensure fundamental freedom to all persons. I should like him to tell us, further, what educational work is being done by the federal government to secure a wider understanding of the principles behind this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to endorse what has been said by my hon. friend from Kootenay West. I have received a number of letters on the same subject, the firing of Miss Smith, from people in my riding as well as from others outside my riding. I think the public in general is entitled to know just what the bill of rights means to them and to what extent it protects them in relation to this matter of free speech. An article appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of May 17 entitled "Bill of Rights Penned on Calfskin". It says:
Copies will be distributed widely. Already there are 15,000 orders for it. The price is likely to be around $1. But nobody will get the bill of rights alone. All will have this extract from Mr. Diefen-baker's speech:
"I am a Canadian, a free Canadian, free to speak without fear, free to worship God in my own way, free to stand for what I think right, free to oppose what X believe wrong, free to choose those who shall govern my country. This heritage of freedom, I pledge to uphold for myself and all mankind."
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that we as Canadians should ask whether this is a right which we now possess, or a law that has been passed enabling individuals to go to court to prove their rights by litigation. If the latter is the case, I suggest this right will not apply to the majority of Canadians at any time, and that they are no better off than before. We in this country have always believed that laws of various kinds, in respect of various subjects, protected the people of this country from violations of the four freedoms which have been fundamental to our way of life. I also suggest that Canadians as a whole believe that the bill of rights is a bill which the government intended to see implemented on behalf of the people of this country so that litigation would be unnecessary to establish those rights, that the rights were inherent to all Canadians.
I have in my hand a copy of a letter from a resident of Alberta where the offence took place to which I have referred. This letter is addressed to my leader.
Who is that, Mr. Douglas?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to read a portion of this letter. The letter is dated May 11, 1961 and reads as follows:
Since you are one of the few M.P.'s who are championing the cause of true Canadianism-
What a laugh that is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this may be a laugh to some hon. members, but I am sure the people of Alberta are well aware that my leader, the hon. member for Assiniboia, is one of the few Canadians who champion the cause of Canadianism.	,
Mr. Chairman, I apologize to the hon. member for Assiniboia. I thought the hon. member for Timiskaming was referring to himself.
The same holds true for the hon. member for Assiniboia.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the letter reads as follows:
Since you are one of the few M.P.'s who are championing the cause of true Canadianism and attempting to restrict the foreign control of our natural resources and way of life, I am enclosing the attached clipping from this morning's local paper.
This is surely in direct contradiction to our bill of rights and everything that we stand for in Canada today and, I thought, the so-called free world.
Mr. Chairman, how is this relevant to the estimates of the Minister of Justice?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suggest we are getting into the problem of deciding whether we are discussing the estimates of the Minister of Justice or the estimates of the Attorney General of Canada, who administers our laws and is responsible for that administration as attorney general. Perhaps the hon. member who made the interjection could inform me that we are discussing only the estimates as applied to the Department of Justice, and thereby solve a problem which has puzzled me for some time. If it is the contention of the hon. member that we are only considering the estimates of the Minister of Justice, I should like the minister to clarify this point. Is the minister the attorney general, as well as the Minister of Justice, serving in the same capacity for Canada in relation to the administration of our laws as the attorney general does in each province?
Having heard nothing from the minister to the contrary, I assume we are discussing his function as attorney general as well as Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that if one looks at the estimates it will be seen that the salaries paid to the Minister of Justice and to the Solicitor General are included in the same estimate. I suggest, therefore, the two should be considered as one department. There are no estimates for the Solicitor General of Canada, except in so far as the estimates of the Department of Justice apply to him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I draw to the attention of the hon. member for Hull that the minister was indicating his responsibilities as Attorney General of Canada, and not those of the Solicitor General of Canada. I think the problem in respect to this point was dealt with in an answer to a question put to the Minister of Justice, on orders of the day, by the hon. member for Skeena. It was indicated at that time that these matters of employment, or the cessation of employment, were matters within the jurisdiction of the provinces, for the reasons advanced at that time. I suggest this involves a question of civil rights, and the administration of justice in this regard is a provincial matter.
Therefore I do not believe that the hon. member is entitled to make reference to a case which is entirely within the jurisdiction of a province. The Minister of Justice is concerned with legislation which is introduced in the house, having regard to the bill of rights, and a discussion in that respect would be relevant. A passing reference to the bill of rights by hon. members could therefore be proper, but a discussion of individual cases over which the minister has no control because they come under the administration of
Supply-Justice
justice within provinces, or perhaps involve civil rights under the jurisdiction of the provinces, would not be relevant. I hope, therefore, hon. members will not discuss the details of problems in respect of provincial jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the Minister of Justice for outlining his duties. That probably represents the information which Canadian people have been looking for to understand his duties having regard to the bill of rights.
I should like to ask whether the bill of rights is of any value as it presently stands, or should it now be included as part of our constitution. I suggest that is not what the Prime Minister indicated when he said that the people of Canada should have the right of freedom of speech in this country. The individual to whom I have referred is a girl who took the opportunity, which was also offered to members of parliament, of going to Cuba during the Easter holidays to examine at length the situation there. Upon her return she attended a meeting of the Knights of the Round Table service club and presented her opinion of what she had seen during her visit to that country. She did this in a manner completely divorced from the field in which she was employed, but was fired as a result.
I would think that when the bill of rights mentions freedom of speech, it includes protection against the loss of one's job. While it is true that the actual loss of employment may be a provincial matter and not fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government, yet it is a fact that we have a bill of rights which the Prime Minister and others have stated will give protection for freedom of speech, freedom of association and the other freedoms inherent in our Canadian way of life. That being so, the bill of rights should guarantee these freedoms to all citizens, and certainly one of the easiest ways to prove that it does not exist is when some company, particularly a company under the domination of the United States oil industry, discharges someone for speaking in a manner that is not detrimental to Canada or even to the company for which the individual works but as he saw things, and for expressing his own views publicly.
I had occasion to watch the program "Close-Up" the other night when this matter was discussed. Three well known and well respected business people from the city of Calgary who took part were of the opinion that the things the lady said probably were harsh. She is a woman 26 years of age. Maybe she was harsh in expressing her opinions on an international matter, but there was nothing wrong in what she said. Nothing was

Supply-Justice
contrary to the good and welfare of Canada itself. I, and I think most citizens of Canada, believe that if the bill of rights is for the protection of our people it should not be necessary for this lady to sue or to do any of the other things that are open to her in the provincial field. She should have the protection of a federal act. I suggest that the responsibility for this situation must rest with the attorney general.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes.
Does the hon. member believe that the freedoms enumerated in the bill of rights include the right to work? Is this not the line on which he is speaking?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I believe the right to employment is the right of every person, and that we should have the opportunity to work. I presume the hon. member is referring to the right to work in another context with which, of course, I disagree. I believe in the right to employment, but that is not the right in question at this time. We are discussing only the rights that appear in the bill of rights.
I believe that changes, amendments or qualifications must be made in the act. Some change must take place in the office of the attorney general so that it will function not only in the prosecuting of people under such legislation as the Combines Investigation Act, through charges laid by the R.C.M.P. and in other fields, but it must work also for the protection of the individual in Canada, to give him the protection that we in the House of Commons thought we gave when we passed the bill of rights. If this is not done, if the bill of rights is not giving these freedoms to everyone as a right, not by litigation or by court procedure, then the bill of rights is a hollow mockery and the country might as well know it. It will be up to the people to make the bill of rights a part of our constitution; then it will be administered as the constitution is administered, and the benefits from it will flow automatically to everyone resident in the country.
There are many other cases that I have been interested in where the attorney general's office, in my opinion, has not functioned as it should. Individuals have made decisions with respect to which the attorney general could act on behalf of the Canadian people, without any need for litigation, if he so desired. I should like to refer to one of those cases. This matter has been brought to my attention and I have communicated with the minister with respect to it. I have made some other inquiries. It has to do with the sale
IMr. Peters.]
of merchandise to some people in this country. This merchandise may or may not be as represented. Companies are being set up- the hon. member can keep on shaking his head as long as he wishes; I am quite well aware of the fact that he does not understand this problem or hardly any other problem. I am not a lawyer. I did not pass the bill of rights to make lawyers rich. My vote helped to pass the bill of rights to see that Canadians received justice without having to go to court. If the bill of rights means that lawyers are going to make a fortune out of it, then may I say that was not my intention.
I received a letter from an individual in my riding referring to knitting machines that were being sold there. This is a case where misrepresentation took place. Many machines were sold. The company either folded up immediately or the individuals left town. The merchandise sold to the people was unsatisfactory. Immediately after the contract was signed it was assigned to another agency, which may or may not be a part of the original organization. The negotiable instrument was sold after the delivery was made. This is the situation that results. The people who receive the merchandise will return it because it is unsatisfactory, but they will still be required to pay for the merchandise itself. I would place one case on the record.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the hon. member continues I should like him to indicate to me how he relates this problem with the estimates of the Department of Justice. I fail to see any relation it may have. It is a problem of the administration of justice, which comes under property and civil rights, which is within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Unless the hon. member is referring to a federal law or a federal act I fail to see how he can be relevant in discussing this matter.

Mr. Chairman, before we proceed I wonder whether I might deal with one matter which I think without question is within the jurisdiction of this department. While it is a question of employee-employer relationships, it is one which comes within the jurisdiction of the federal government and has a relationship with the bill of rights. The case has been well publicized in the newspapers because of the unique situation which existed. Questions have been asked in the house about it, and documents relating to this particular incident have been tabled.
I am referring specifically to what I consider to be an abrogation of that which has been classified in the bill of rights as freedom of association, and specifically to a Mr. Terry Whitfield who was summarily dismissed by

Canadian Marconi Company under a clause in their contract of employment, which is completely contrary to that part of the bill of rights relating to freedom of association.
The Marconi company wrote to Mr. Whitfield with respect to this matter on April 12, 1961, under the signature of Mr. S. M. Finlay-son, the president. I should like to read the relevant part of this letter if I may, Mr. Chairman, to indicate what I mean. It is addressed to Mr. Whitfield, c/o Canadian Marconi Company, R.C.A.F. Station, Great Whale River, Box 6121, Montreal, and reads:
Dear Mr. Whitfield:
Since receipt last week of your letter dated the 27th ultimo I have had an investigation made of the circumstances relating to your employment to which it alludes and am now in a position to reply.
Under the terms of your employment agreement, set out in the letter of November 2, 1960, addressed to you by Mr. R. MacLeod, manager of our special services division, and signed and accepted by you the following day, it was expressly provided:
Then he quotes the section from that particular contract:
Native and Eskimo villages are considered out of bounds and personnel are prohibited from fraternization or association with the native populations except in special circumstances. Infringement of these orders is cause for discharge.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. While this subject may be relevant in another context, I fail to see how a contract of employment can be a subject of discussion under the estimates of the Department of Justice, even though there may be rights under the bill of rights which should be invoked on behalf of the individual. The individual must invoke those rights by an action against his employer. This is a contract of employment. I feel, therefore, that the discussion of this subject is not germane, although it may be in another context. I submit that all this discussion is out of order.

If I may comment on the point of order raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West, I should like to indicate what the bill of rights says in this respect. I quote section 1, as follows:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely-
Then there is an enumeration of a number of them, and paragraph (e) says:
(e) freedom of assembly and association;
The Minister of Justice was one who participated in the passage of this particular act under which he has certain responsibilities. The act declares that certain conditions have existed, and I merely point out this particular incident as an example of something
Supply-Justice
that is contrary to the provisions in the bill of rights. This incident shows these conditions have not existed and do not exist in respect of Mr. Whitfield and Miss Witalktuk, the young lady to whom he is engaged and whose association with him caused his dismissal.
I submit that it is entirely in order to discuss the subject from the point of view of justice to this individual. If the bill of rights means anything at all, if the minister has any obligation whatever in this regard, certainly it is in order to discuss this obviously callous and arrogant treatment by the Canadian Marconi Company of Mr. Whitfield, which is completely contrary to the provisions of the bill of rights. If we cannot discuss it here, if it is not a question of justice to this individual, where can we discuss it? Perhaps we can discuss it outside the house, as we are able to do on so many occasions when hon. gentlemen opposite object to things being debated here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member must realize that he is in the House of Commons of Canada and must discuss matters which are within the province of the federal parliament. I suggest that he is not free to discuss matters which come within provincial jurisdiction. He is free to discuss those matters outside of this house.
In so far as the bill of rights is concerned, this bill does not apply to matters within the jurisdiction of the provinces. As I indicated before, the matter of employment involves a civil right which is clearly within the jurisdiction of the provinces, as is the administration of justice. I feel, therefore, that the hon. member cannot really discuss subjects of that kind on the estimates of the Department of Justice. I would not say there would not be other occasions on which the problem of the bill of rights could be discussed in general, but certainly not in the way the hon. member for Skeena is seeking to do and as the hon. member for Timis-kaming sought to do earlier. I rule, therefore, that in the way this discussion has been going up to the moment, it is not relevant.
In order to clarify the situation, Mr. Chairman, may I ask if the Minister of Justice is responsible to the house for the bill of rights?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In relation to those matters indicated in the bill of rights. For instance, when legislation is brought before the house it must be examined by the Minister of Justice in order that he may determine that there is nothing within the legislation contrary to the bill of rights.

There is another question that I should like to put. If a member wants to

Supply-Justice
ask the minister whether there is any possibility of amending the bill of rights, in view of the conflict between provincial and federal rights, would that be within the rules of this house?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I fail to see how the hon. member, by directing a question to the Minister of Justice during the discussion of the departmental estimates, could force the minister to impose any obligation on the provinces to implement the bill of rights within those provinces, or to direct that a provincial bill of rights be enacted. This is certainly not the responsibility of the minister. I think this case is clearly in the same position as the one that has been discussed, which clearly was not the concern of the Minister of Justice. It seems to me that this discussion is clearly irrelevant.

I think there has been a misunderstanding about what we are getting at in this particular case to which I referred, the relationship between Mr. Whitfield and the Canadian Marconi Company and his discharge because of this fraternization clause. I submit the matter is within the jurisdiction of this federal parliament because Mr. Whitfield was working for the Canadian Marconi Company, which company has a contract with the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources for certain activities near Great Whale river. It is this relationship that I was getting at. Here is an individual working for a company-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand the point that the hon. member is trying to make. It may be a problem for discussion with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources to ascertain what the department can do about a practice like that from an administrative point of view when it gives a contract to a company. However, the employment by Canadian Marconi of any person in the execution of this contract is certainly not a problem that is related in any way to the Minister of Justice or the Attorney General of Canada on these estimates; that is another matter. There may be an administrative problem to discuss with the minister concerned but, as the hon. member has clearly indicated, the employment contract is between a company and an individual and has nothing to do with the Minister of Justice. It is a private matter between the Canadian Marconi Company and the individual in question.

What I was leading into was an attempt to show where the bill of rights is deficient in this regard-the Attorney General of Canada has some responsibility in some fields, even though it is not precisely clear just what they all are-in not providing 
some machinery in the Department of Justice to enable Mr. Whitfield to find some solution to the grievance he has apart from spending all his time and money wandering around the courts attempting to deal with a monopolistic outfit like the Canadian Marconi Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A number of points have been raised this morning. If I may, I will start with the point made by the hon. member for Megantic with regard to an apparent discrepancy between the totals shown in the second column of the blue book for this year as having been the expenditure by the department for 1960-61 and the totals as he arrived at them by adding up what was shown in the main estimates for last year plus various supplementary estimates. As I recall it, he pointed out that the discrepancy between the two totals was something of the order of $800,000 and asked me for an explanation.
The explanation I have is this. In the estimates for last year-that is for 1960-61 -provision for salary revision for all the public service was made in one place, namely in the general salaries vote of the Department of Finance. In other words, the increase in expenditure that resulted from the salary increase which was approved last year, and amounted to many millions of dollars, was last year asked for under one item in the estimates of the Department of Finance.
Of course that would not give the true picture of the expenditures by departments, because the increase for convenience let us say it was in the neighbourhood of $40 million, although I am not saying that it was that amount-would obviously be divided, with so many million dollars to this department and so many million dollars to each of the other departments. When the book of main estimates was made up for this year, in order to reflect what was felt to be a truer picture, the amount of the salary increase attributable to each department was added to the amount shown in the second column in the book so that the amount in the second column in the book this year-that is the amount that is reported to have been spent last year-includes the portion of

Supply-J ustice
the salary increase attributable to the respective departments. But in last year's main and supplementary estimate none of it was shown as attributable to a specific department; it was all lumped in the Department of Finance estimates in a single item. I am told that the difference this year accounts for an amount of $861,004, and I think that is the difference to which the hon. gentleman was directing our attention.
The hon. member for Peace River raised two matters in connection with possible amendments to the Criminal Code. He drew attention to what he considers to be a situation which makes it desirable to amend section 722 of the code. I have to say that it is not our intention to make an amendment to this section this year. The Criminal Code amendment bill is practically ready, and it does not include an amendment which would cover that suggestion. However, we will certainly give it careful consideration for another year.
With respect to the second suggestion the hon. member made, I am glad to be able to say that in our study of this matter we have come to the conclusion that his suggestion is a proper one; that is, that there should be an amendment to the code in connection with offences committed while driving an automobile. I am confident that when my hon. friend sees the Criminal Code amendment bill he will approve of the amendment which we have included in that respect.
There was a considerable amount of discussion on the bill of rights and its application to one or two specific cases which were mentioned. You have ruled, Mr. Chairman, that in as much as it is not the responsibility of the Minister of Justice or Attorney General of Canada to enforce the bill of rights on behalf of individuals, particularly where the right concerned is within provincial jurisdiction, this is not a matter which should be discussed on the estimates of this department.
With that ruling I of course agree, but perhaps, I might, without violating your ruling, Mr. Chairman, refer to one part of the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West, who asked me what is being done to persuade the provinces to take similar action in their fields. This in my view would be the answer which hon. members who have raised these cases are seeking. If the provinces would enact similar bills of rights in their fields of jurisdiction-that is, similar to the bill of rights in the federal field-the whole field of rights and freedoms in Canada would be covered. It seems to me this is a desirable thing and I hope that the case in Calgary may serve as a further incentive, a further spur to citizens in the provinces to

urge upon their governments, and finally urge successfully, that they too should adopt bills of rights which would be effective within the field of provincial jurisdiction.
For the rest, Mr. Chairman, the fact of the matter is that it was carefully explained at the time the bill of rights was before the house that the courts are an integral and essential part of the protection of our rights. All the legislature can do is define the rights and put them in statute form, which is a very effective form, to show that these rights exist and are the legislative entitlement of the Canadian people.
However, it was carefully explained by me in the course of the debate on the bill of rights that the courts were an essential part of the protection of our rights, and that if it was felt these rights may have been violated and should be asserted, protection or restitution should be sought from the courts.
Therefore hon. members should not feel they have been taken by surprise when they find this to be the situation. Of course it would be quite intolerable to take seriously the suggestion hon. members made-I am not relating this to any specific case-that the Minister of Justice or Attorney General of Canada should himself be responsible for deciding when a Canadian citizen's rights had been violated and what should be done to protect them.
I can understand their views when, as they view it, a large and powerful company is at fault here. However, let me ask these hon. members to consider the implications of what they are suggesting. I am quite sure they would resent it very deeply indeed if I made a finding that one of them, for instance, had violated the rights of somebody else and if I brought a prosecution myself and attempted to determine in what respect restitution should be made.
This, of course, is a matter for the courts. It would be an intolerable situation if the Minister of Justice or Attorney General were to accept this invitation and set himself up as an arbiter in cases where he felt a right had been violated. That would be a dictatorship; that is exactly what the bill of rights was designed to protect against, and it is something which this government would never allow, once it brought-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. My point of order is that the minister is deliberately misconstruing the remarks made from this side of the chamber in order to paint an incorrect picture. While the minister may be trained in the use of words, he is using his position as minister to do this. It is most unkind and most unfair.
nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend does not like to have the logical conclusion of his suggestion drawn to his attention. But that is what I am doing; I am drawing to his attention the logical conclusion of the suggestion he has made and the position that he and the hon. member for Timiskaming have taken in this respect.
The hon. member for Skeena also asked about the responsibilities of the Solicitor General. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I might just finish this subject before one o'clock. I direct the hon. member's attention again to the answer given by the Prime Minister, which was referred to in debate by the hon. member and by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert on May 19, just a week ago.
That, I think, is a complete answer; but to give some more particulars I can of course say that the Solicitor General is individually responsible for the review of all cases where the question of commutation of the death sentence arises. He is in charge of the review of cases generally where the exercise of the royal prerogative of mercy is concerned, including the remission of fines and forfeitures, temporary releases from prison for compassionate reasons, applications for ordinary pardons and a number of other matters of that type, the submissions on which are numerous and involve a great deal of careful and very detailed consideration, research and comparison.
In addition to these particular duties, as the Prime Minister pointed out in his answer last week, the Solicitor General undertakes such assignments as may be referred to him as a member of cabinet, and of course he does act as Minister of Justice whenever the Minister of Justice happens to be away. I am not away too frequently, but there are occasions where official business takes me away. For instance, I was with the Prime Minister in London for ten days this year. During the period of negotiation of the Columbia river treaty I was frequently absent because of attendance in Victoria and Washington. On these and similar occasions the Solicitor General acts as Minister of Justice.
Therefore I think my hon. friend can set his mind at rest on the point of whether or not the Solicitor General, by his industry and by the importance of the tasks which he performs, merits the salary which is provided for him.

On May 20, 1958, I brought up in this house the question of goof balls. At that time I was laughed at and sneered at by everyone-I see one hon. member sneering now-but I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, that the goof ball problem when I made reference to it then was a serious problem and that today it is a calamity in Canada.
Yesterday my colleague from St. Denis asked the Minister of Justice a question about what the government is doing in connection with this goof ball problem-he called it the barbiturate problem-and the minister replied, saying that while the hon. member was talking the government was acting. As I have just mentioned, I raised this subject in the house on May 20, 1958 and here is the minister saying in 1961, three years later, that the government was acting, that they were not talking. Well, if this is an example of the speed at which this government acts, then God help us poor Canadians. As I said, I brought the matter up in May, 1958, and today the minister tells us three years later, that they are acting. What were they doing in the meantime? They have spent three years doing nothing. For three years they stood idly by watching a problem, which could easily have been settled then, grow to a point where it must be considered as a national problem almost impossible of solution.
When I spoke on goof balls in May, 1958, the then chief of the inspection services of the Department of National Health and Welfare gave an interview to a newspaper saying there was no goof ball problem. He said he did not take seriously the term "goof ball". "I heard that one 30 years ago", he said. I said then that this official of the Department of National Health and Welfare must either have been asleep at the switch or trying to avoid his responsibility. I have here hundreds of clippings and editorials from Canadian newspapers dealing with the seriousness of the goof ball problem and urging that prompt measures be taken to combat it. Yet this official, this man who should have been on the alert, instead of investigating whether

what I had said in the house was true, promptly denied my statement, claiming that there was no such thing as a goof ball problem.

Mr. Chairman, I am concerned with the goof ball problem because it has been suggested by police officers, who have dealt with the problem on different occasions, that it is a more serious problem than the narcotic problem. Mr. Chairman, at the point I was interrupted I was in the process of suggesting that the government could very easily have put an end to this illegal traffic some three years ago when the situation was brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice.
The use of goof balls has become a plague which is undermining the youth of our country. This fact was brought to the attention of the Department of Justice some three years
Supply-Justice
ago, and I suggest that department should have taken it into consideration, enacted legislation making it illegal for pushers to sell these goof balls to the youth in our schools and elsewhere. However, at that time the government did nothing in this regard. Now, three years later, the Minister of Justice announces that it is intended that measures be found to combat this serious menace.
I suggest the use of goof balls is the first step toward drug addiction. Boys and girls from 12 to 18 years of age-perfect boys and girls-can become criminals over night through the use of goof balls which they are able to purchase at confectionery stores and ice cream parlours. If a boy or girl consumes a bottle of gingerale, or other similar drink, in which has been placed a goof ball, he or she is quite capable of committing murder or carrying out any other similar terrible crime. Three years ago there were three or four hundred girls and boys who were using goof balls. The government has done nothing to correct this situation, and today I suggest there are thousands of young boys and girls across this country who have fallen far down the social ladder through the use of goof balls. Nothing has been done to prevent men and women from despoiling our youth by selling them goof balls.
Authorities in Montreal have become alarmed by the growth of this goof ball traffic. They have called together scientists, statistical men, doctors, and other learned individuals in an attempt to find out what can be done to eradicate this evil. I understand that representations have been made to the Minister of National Health and Welfare in respect to a meeting to be held in Ottawa to discuss this situation. As long ago as May 20, 1958 I suggested in this house that the confectionery and ice cream parlours where these goof balls were being sold, should be kept under surveillance in an attempt to find out who the pushers were, with the intention of adopting measures to stop these harmful transactions. As I said a moment or two ago, nothing has been done.
I should like to direct hon. members' attention to an article which appeared in Time magazine of March 31, 1958, which I quoted in my remarks in this house on June 27, 1958, as reported at page 1700 of Hansard for that day. This article indicated that a young man, 14 years of age, died in Halifax from an overdose of goof balls which he had taken from the drug store where he was employed as a messenger. When this young man got home that evening his folks found that he acted strangely, as if he were drunk and foolish. Next day he went out for a walk and disappeared. Three weeks later his

body was found in a wooded area near his home. The verdict of the coroner's jury was barbiturate poisoning.

In this article it was stated that an investigation had revealed that four dozen goof balls, barbiturate pills, had been smuggled into the prison on Sunday by a visitor. If a few goof balls smuggled into a prison or a penitientiary will bring about the devastation that those brought about, namely the smashing of the wing of the jail, then just imagine what a gang of young hoodlums provided with goof balls will do.

K.C.M.P. authorities have received over 20 complaints about young people who had been using sedatives or barbiturates, commonly known as goof balls.

May I speak to the point of order? Surely, it is not the responsibility of the chairman to interpret the feelings of the committee in so far as the granting of additional time is concerned. This is something that requires unanimous consent. If unanimous consent is not given, then no extension of time is allowed. I do not believe it is the responsibility of the Chair to interpret what might be the attitude of the committee.

I was
only pointing out what the practice of the committee normally is. I was not making any ruling. If the question is put to me, I will put it to the committee. Has the hon. member unanimous consent of the committee to continue?

I want to say just a few words on this question of goof balls. I should like to refer the Chair to an article that appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of March 8, 1961, under the heading, "Brief to Fulton; Police Want Laws Changed". This article refers to seven recommendations with which I shall not deal in detail. However, recommendation No. 4 reads:
Inclusion under the vagrancy section of unemployed drug addicts who do not have a doctor's certificate declaring them unable to work.
At this time. I wish to ask the minister to study the matter to ascertain if it is feasible to include in the amendments which will be introduced to the Criminal Code a section in the vagrancy provision that will take care of drug addicts and so on.

Last night, Mr. Chairman, I had the opportunity of reading some words of one of the admirers of the minister. I am going to take advantage of the opportunity today to read another account in praise of the minister in order to give me another point from which to ask him a question or two. This is from a great admirer of the minister, Pat Nicholson, who puts out an Ottawa report for the Thomson papers. The heading in the Port Arthur newspaper of May 23 is, "Give High Rating For Davie Fulton".
Oh, oh.

I am only going to read a couple of paragraphs which I know will delight the minister and his backers. I am glad to see them here today. The article reads in part:
Thousands of words have flowed over his lips since that cold December day, only 4] years ago, when British Columbia's own Davie Fulton challenged John Diefenbaker for the leadership of the Conservative party.
But those words, unlike water flowing downstream to the sea, have not been lost. Dammed behind some personal wall of determination, they have gently but surely accumulated into a powerhouse of countrywide good will and respect for their speaker.
I know his colleagues in the committee will forgive me for leaving out a few paragraphs that are along the same general lines, but then we get down to this:
Davie Fulton without question possesses the finest intellect in the cabinet today. For pure mental training and intellectual stature, he has no equal.
Then, I go on to this particular paragraph:
He is, ex officio, the minister in charge of the R.C.M.P. In this role, he has had pleasant and unpleasant duties to perform, gaining the most headlines, perhaps, by his action in refusing to send R.C.M.P. reinforcements to Newfoundland
[The Acting Chairman.]
when requested to do so by Liberal Premier Joey Smallwood who sought their aid in the labour dispute in that province.
Just as an aside, I should like to congratulate the minister on the strong fight he must have put up in the cabinet in order to obtain support for not sending police into Newfoundland.
Going on in the article, we come to this phrase. Mr. Nicholson suggests the minister could have been a hero if he had gone to British Columbia and taken over the leadership of the Conservative party there but, as the author says:
-he chose to remain in Ottawa, from which strategic centre he breaks out to deliver good fighting speeches to public audiences, campaigning for his government and for his own future, showing that he can call on wit, derision, learning, common sense, farsightedness and rhetoric to uplift and persuade his audience.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this article sets out, perhaps properly and perhaps accurately, an estimate of the minister's worth. I certainly am not going to gainsay or deny this. But in view of this breadth and ability that the minister seems to have, I want to turn to one small point and ask him whether he has considered looking at the operations of other departmental offices or ministerial offices as a basis of comparison in order to see whether perhaps it has developed that, because of his general brilliance in an over-all way, he has not looked at the little details of his own department in order to see how things go through his office.
I do not have much contact with the minister but I am always astounded at how long it takes to get a reply from his office. If you get one in three weeks, I think you are doing very well. Not long ago I pointed out to the minister that a man in Sault Ste. Marie had written to him complaining that the R.C.M.P. had broken into his home and had messed things up. The minister has satisfied him and I suppose other people that the R.C.M.P. were not the ones involved. But the point is that six weeks after the man had written to the minister he had received no reply from the minister's office. I do not care whether he is the worst and lowest thug in Canada, any person who writes to the minister surely deserves a more prompt reply than that. I am not going to speak for other members but from conversations I have had with others I know that they report that same pattern in so far as this department is concerned. It takes much more than the ordinary length of time to get any kind of response to a request either by phone or by letter.
I am just wondering whether the minister would not check into this phase of his operations. It would be dreadful if we had his

continued build up on lines that Mr. Nicholson has set forth and yet right within his own office there were a situation in which the satisfaction that perhaps might be deserved, was not being given by him or his personnel. I might appear to be flippant in bringing this matter before the committee. However, I would suggest to the minister that it would be a worth while thing upon which to check. If you write to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Transport, the Minister of National Revenue or the Postmaster General you get a reply in from three to five days or someone contacts you in the office. But in this department with this brilliant head you wait and wait. This is just a minor detail of administration but I thought it would be worth while to bring it to the minister's attention. I know that he would like to live up to-and perhaps he does so- all these elaborate assessments that have been given by such astute observers as Mr. Nicholson.
The hon. member for Skeena somewhat misinterpreted the question that I had asked the minister yesterday and to which I did not receive a reply. The hon. member for Skeena wanted to know whether with regard to these legal jobs or legal fees the minister would make a statement to the effect that they had not been given to Conservative party members. What I really was seeking was an assurance that they had been given to supporters or members of the Conservative party. But much more important than that, I wonder whether the minister would give us some information on the matter I raised in relation to amending procedure in connection with the British North America Act.
He will recall that at the dominion-provincial conference in July last year, at one of the afternoon sessions the Prime Minister made this matter one of the central points and stressed very strongly that the procedure to amend the constitution was one of the most vital things ahead of the nation as a whole. Subsequently, there were a number of meetings which received a considerable amount of publicity and last night I suggested that some of these left a very vague impression as to what was happening and what were the difficulties. Before the minister leaves this part of his estimates I should like him to bring us up to date on that matter.
The last point that comes to my mind results from the minister's explanation of the difficulty with the bill of rights. He pointed out that if he was expected as attorney general or Minister of Justice to take up every case in which someone felt that someone was infringing or impinging upon his rights, he would be involved in extremely great difficulty. I wonder whether the minister or
Supply-Justice
the government has given any consideration to a practice that has been developed in other parts of the western world and has received a certain amount of critical acclaim from journalists, academic people and even editorial writers. I refer to the idea of an office similar to that of ombudsman that has been worked out in several of the Scandinavian countries where there is an office created by the government but separate from it to which anyone can take any appeal for any injustice that he feels he has suffered through legislation or impingement of government activities.
I realize that a federal government can properly deal only with things that fall within the federal framework. But when we have so much delegated authority as we have today, it seems to me that this procedure becomes more and more a worth while possibility. I wonder whether the minister has given any consideration to the matter, whether this has been a subject of discussion with the executive of this government, whether he has had any memoranda prepared on it or whether anyone in the government has studied how it works in other parts of the world.
The last point upon which I wish to touch under this item is the question of where the minister stands in connection with appointing justices in relation to the article or editorial in the Montreal Gazette from which I quoted last night which indicated that this government had a marvellous chance to follow the line indicated by the Prime Minister when he was in office, namely to make the prime factor in appointing a justice his merit or ability rather than his political colour. I wanted to ask the minister where this particular government stands in this regard.

Speaking to the point of order, may I say that I did not say that. I was referring to Mr. Nicholson, one of the fearless members of the press gallery. This was

his interpretation. My whole point in reading this article was not to raise this problem but rather to underline the valiant stand taken by the minister probably within the cabinet to make sure that the mounted police did not go to Newfoundland.

Like some other departments in the government, the Department of Justice has certain small statutory expenditures presumably to pay pensions to widows or to deceased employees. These expenditures are not discussed under any estimates. I want to ask the Minister of Justice by what authority this fund was set up covering statutory expenditures. I always presumed it was by reason of an order in council.
I notice one item in the estimates of the Department of Justice for an amount of $2,400. This $2,400 is to pay annual pensions to three widows in respect of their husbands who lost their lives in the performance of their duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. member to which item he is referring? I have not located it and I wonder whether the hon. member could give me the item number.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Thank you.

Two of these widows receive an annual pension of $900 each and the third widow receives an annual pension of $600. I do not know when these pensions were determined or how long they have been paid to these particular widows. They seem small in relation to the increased cost of living and increased pensions. Mr. Chairman, as I was saying a short time ago, on May 20, 1958, I asked that cases made against pushers or drug addicts using goof balls be changed from the Department of National Health and Welfare and placed under the Criminal Code or some other law so that the R.C.M.P. could act under it, take these people in and prevent further distribution if possible.
All hon. members can see this article. "Goof balls" is big enough there for anybody

to see; it occupies almost half a page. This is La Patrie du Dimanche of February 19, 1961 and the title of the article is:
(Translation):
Alarming situation
Goof balls available to high school students.
(Text):
That is, "Goof balls on the road of scholars". The article has five by-lines, but I will only read one because it is a very lengthy article:
(Translation):
Doctor and two nurses assaulted by patient, 15, in Notre Dame hospital.
Within a few days, riots in Montreal jail and St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary.
Woman murdered on St. Lawrence blvd., her assaillant hardly aware of what he was doing.
Within a few months, four in morgue due to poisoning.
Damage by goof balls, which represent an increasingly complex problem for justice and are the main enemy of order and public rest.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are five subheadings which reveal the damage wrought by goof balls and are evidence of the fact that those crimes were committed under the effect of goof balls.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether 1 could ask the hon. member a question. Would the hon. member please define "goof ball" for me? I do not know what it is. Will the hon. member tell me exactly what is in it and how it works?
I am not a druggist and 1 cannot tell the hon. member what it contains. The users purchase these goof balls from druggists, I presume, or obtain them through some other channel.
But I would like to know what it is. What is it? Is it made up of bread and butter, or castor oil, or Epsom salts, or what is it? What is in it?

Mr. Chairman. I wonder whether the answer to that question could perhaps be given by my hon. friend's colleague who was applauding so loudly a moment ago and who is a member of the medical profession.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, does this not demonstrate pretty clearly that this question should be discussed under the estimates of the department of my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who will have the officials here who can give us all this information?
The minister-

The Minister of Justice-

Order; I am already on my feet. I am inclined to the view I have already given to the committee. To some extent the hon. member was touching on the Department of Justice at various times and that was the reason why I permitted him to continue. But this is really a discussion of a social problem and it is the direct administrative responsibility of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The hon. member will have an opportunity to present his case when the estimates of that department are before the committee. To the extent to which the hon. member is referring to the importation of drugs or trafficking in narcotics over the border, or bringing them in from other countries as was discussed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, I think it was, yesterday, this would appear to be applicable to the discussion.
Therefore I would ask the hon. member to limit his remarks to matters which are the direct administrative responsibility of the minister. With regard to that portion of his remarks which concern the responsibility of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the hon. member can deal with that matter at a later date.
(Translation):

Let me explain that in our view, the situation created by the use of goof balls is so alarming that it constitutes a problem for the Minister of Justice. We are seeking amendments to the Criminal Code to place barbituates on the same footing as drugs and put them under the same control of the R.C.M.P. In making this request, we find it necessary, to bolster our arguments-and I feel the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean is completely in order-to establish the seriousness and dire social consequences resulting from the use of those barbiturates at the present time.
Therefore, I think the minister should tell us whether he soon proposes to bring forward amendments to the Criminal Code in an effort to stop the damage caused by this serious problem.
(Text):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, you have referred to the question of relevancy and I think there is also the question of repetition to be considered at this stage.
