The hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean has pointed out the situation and now he persists in repeating the same thing in all sorts of colours and guises. He is not really adding anything to what his colleagues, the hon. member for Megantic and others, have already said. His colleagues have said the same thing, and I think that on the point of repetition the hon. member should be ruled out of order, as well as on the question of his remarks not being relevant to the matter under discussion.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, some time ago, a question was directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare about the review which could be made to solve the problem of the use of barbiturates, known as "goof balls".
At the time, the minister said he was considering the matter in co-operation with the authorities of the Department of Justice. Therefore, it is impossible to solve that problem without the co-operation of both departments.
I did not have time to read the page of Hansard where the matter is recorded, but I have a good memory and I recall what the minister said. He stated that the authorities of the Department of Justice had to be consulted to introduce legislation. Therefore, they are closely related in this matter. Furthermore, he cannot deny that the Department of Justice has some interest in the matter. Now, the hon. member is specifically asking the Minister of Justice to see to it that the matter be placed under the Criminal Code, in order that the R.C.M.P. may intervene in the matter, like in the matter of any other barbiturate. Consequently, I submit that the hon. member is not out of order.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to the argument put forward by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, I must say that the situation should first of all be cleared and that no member in this house considers the seriousness of the goof ball problem. But when the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont states that the Minister of Justice is the person qualified to hear the grievances of this house, I do not think that we can share his views because the use of goof balls cannot be considered as an unlawful action punishable under the Criminal Code before any legal definition is given of what goof balls are.
Then, let him do it.

The hon. member for St. Denis says; Let him do it. Any amendment to the food and drugs act must be introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

Supply-J ustice
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare has stated that barbiturates or goof-balls are drugs, the Criminal Code will then be amended accordingly and a provision to this effect will be included therein. Then, from the moment on, all transactions, sales or use of goof balls will constitute a crime and the Minister of Justice will have the authority to reply to the arguments raised by the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean.
For the time being, we respectfully submit that the hon. member has no right to deal with goof balls.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wonder if I could help to dispose of the point of order in a helpful manner and, indeed, dispose of the discussion as well by pointing out that as I understand the case of those who support the right of hon. members to speak about goof balls, it is that they were urging that we should place them under the provisions of the Criminal Code in the same way, one of them said, as narcotics presently are. May I point out that this is an entirely erroneous approach. Narcotics are not under the Criminal Code. There is a separate act-the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act-which is administered by my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare who is responsible for dealing with discussions concerning that measure. With regard to goof balls, I have referred repeatedly to what my colleague has said, namely, that he intends to introduce legislation to amend the Food and Drugs Act so as to deal with goof balls. That, again, will not be an amendment to the Criminal Code, and the responsibility of introducing and administering that act will be that of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Because this question does not come under my administrative responsibility I have no officials here who can advise me. It is, in my submission, irrelevant to my department. Perhaps if hon. members would understand and appreciate the point that we are introducing legislation in the form of an amendment to the Food and Drugs Act, and that the question was never then, nor is it now, one of my administrative responsibilities, they will understand why I have endeavoured to point out, reasonably, I hope, that this is not a matter upon which I can be helpful. However, they can obtain all the information they feel they should have if they will wait until the appropriate time.
In connection with the length of time which has elapsed before bringing down legislation, I know that some hon. members are concerned about that, but we have been concerned about it, too. It is, of course, easy

to assume an expert knowledge, but I can assure hon. members opposite that expert knowledge on the subject is not easy to come by and when you are dealing with a drug which, when properly used, is a legitimate aid to medicine you do not lightly pass laws outlawing it and making its possession illegal. This question must be approached on the basis of knowing that the measures taken are appropriate ones, that they are acceptable and that they will be enforceable. I know this has been one of the problems of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I can assure hon. members it is not a case of simply writing an act and producing it within a month or two. There is more to be done in connection with this problem than might appear on the surface. However, my hon. friend has been working on this matter in conjunction with other departments that are in a position to advise him and his officials, and is now in a position to introduce legislation into this house next week if not earlier. At that time the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean and others interested can get the fullest explanation, the fullest accounting of how the legislation will work. I am sorry, but I am unable to advise them on that point, with the best will in the world. So I suggest again that having had a fairly full reference made to this problem it might be considered appropriate to leave it either until the estimates of the other department are discussed or until the bill itself is introduced.
May I take advantage of this occasion to reply to some of the questions which have been asked on other subjects since I last rose to reply. The hon. member for Port Arthur praised me with one hand and damned me with the other. There is no objection to that on my part. I do recall that I had occasion once to admit to him that there had been delay in sending a reply to a letter, and I explained to him then some of the circumstances accounting for the delay. It was due to my absence at the moment when the reply was being prepared, and again after it had been prepared.
I was not aware there was a general feeling that correspondence from my office was slow. I will certainly look into that question and do what I can to remedy any defects. It may be that one reason why, in some cases, some extra time is taken to answer letters is that many deal with problems of a legal nature to which a swift reply cannot readily be given. It is one thing to send replies on subjects which deal with statistics, where all that is needed is to look up the record on the basis of the actual figures, and altogether another to deal with the great majority of

the communications which I receive, in connection with which time and care are necessary in order to prepare a suitable answer.
Another reason which may account tor some delay is that I have made a rule, perhaps erroneously, that I should answer every letter which comes to my office. I am not referring to letters directed to the department. But when somebody writes to me, whether it is a member of parliament or somebody outside the house, I do like to send a reply. This is the general rule, and I have laid it down because I feel that people who write to a minister are entitled to an answer signed by the minister. I do not say this is done in every case, but it is my general approach. I must confess that on occasions this has had the result that there is more correspondence for my signature than I am able to keep up with, especially on occasions when I have been absent from Ottawa for fairly lengthy periods. I think perhaps I may have to modify that approach to see that interim acknowledgement goes out, signed by someone else. I shall have to look at the situation to see what can be done to remedy this dissatisfaction. My approach has been that every letter addressed to me is entitled to a reply from me, and I have always felt the reply should be carefully considered. For that reason, as well as the others which I have given, I should not deny that I may on occasion have been rather more behind with my correspondence than perhaps I should have been.
A further question was raised regarding the appointment of agents of the Minister of Justice and judges. I am not sure which point of view the hon. member for Port Arthur takes in respect of the appointment of agents-lawyers to act for or on behalf of judges. That hon. member has expressed a different approach today from that which I understood him to take yesterday. May I assure him, as well as other hon. members of this committee, that the criterion which is followed is, that agents of the Minister of Justice must be the most competent and proper persons in the field to represent the Minister of Justice in the carriage of litigation on behalf of the crown and the government of Canada. I have received criticism on occasion in that these persons, who were appointed as agents, have not always and inevitably been individuals who have been associated with me in a political way. I have not received very many criticisms of this kind, but I have received some.
In respect of the appointment of judges, we follow the same standard, in that a very high calibre must be secured in respect of each appointment to the bench. I have not
Supply-J ustice
made a statistical examination, or even attempted to make an analysis, of what may be the affiliation of those individuals we have appointed, because we attempt to avoid the influence of that factor upon our decisions. We try to obtain the best men available.
I can refer to one individual we elevated to the Supreme Court of Canada, who was a judge appointed to the Ontario bench by our predecessors. I am sure if I made an analysis I should find other similar cases. However, our approach has always been that members appointed to the bench must be the best men available for the job. That is the only criterion that we follow.
The hon. member for Port Arthur raised the question regarding the appointment of some one equivalent to an ombudsman in the Scandinavian countries, to carry out his functions in respect of our bill of rights. We did consider this matter very thoroughly, both at the time the bill of rights was being prepared and presented to the house, and since. While not rejecting the suggestion in principle, we felt that it is not capable of direct application to Canada, which is a country with a federal system. Outsiders may feel there is rather an anomalous situation in Canada, in that the criminal law is enacted by the federal parliament while its enforcement and administration are matters of provincial responsibility. The type of complaints with which I understand the ombudsman deals in Scandinavian countries are closely connected with the enforcement of criminal law, and it seemed to us it would not be an acceptable situation, in view of the provincial enforcement of criminal law, to have an individual, who fancied himself aggrieved, appealing to the federal government through an ombudsman, because of their complaint against the enforcement of the law by the provinces, which are responsible for that enforcement. I recognize, however, that an ombudsman is not confined to matters of criminal law, and that the suggestion is made that such an individual might also be useful in the function of reviewing administrative procedures of the federal government itself, in the enforcement of statutes which are the responsibility of the federal government. We have considered this suggestion but have felt, to the present time at any rate, that there is no indication that we cannot produce an equally satisfactory result, through a very careful check by the minister and the Department of Justice of legislation which is introduced, and a readiness to review any complaints which may be made with respect to actions of other departments. It is appreciated, of course, that I cannot direct other departments or veto their actions. We have had a number of cases of complaints being made

Supply-J ustice
regarding other departments, at which time I have discussed these complaints with my colleagues on the basis of there being no objection to my discussing it with them, with the intention of reviewing and examining the complaint to see if there is anything involved which is contrary to the spirit as well as the letter of the bill of rights. In a number of cases we have made very extensive reviews of the activities of other departments on that basis.
It must always be borne in mind that the Minister of Justice cannot dictate in these matters. However, we have had no indication, as yet, that there is any serious gap as a result of this system which would necessitate the appointment of anyone in the nature of an ombudsman in this country. For those two reasons-the peculiarities of the federal system, and the fact that we have taken pains to review our own activities, as a government-I suggest that, as yet at any rate, we are not satisfied that there is any need for such an appointment.
The hon. member for Welland asked me about the authority for a statutory item appearing at the bottom of page 36, which provides $2,400 for pensions to dependents of penitentiary personnel, who lost their lives in the performance of their duty. In the first case there was a statute of 1914 which authorized the payment of an allowance of $500 to a Mrs. Jointson, the widow of an officer employed at the British Columbia penitentiary. This amount was increased by $400 in the main estimates of 1959-60, so that it was only last year that Mrs. Jointson's annual pension was increased from $500 to $900.
The second case involved a widow of another guard employed at the British Columbia penitentiary, and by an item appearing in the estimates, which was incorporated under the Appropriation Acts in 1927, this lady was granted an annual allowance of $600 commencing April 1, 1937. Last year we increased that amount by $300, making a total of $900, to continue during her natural life.
The third case was in respect to the widow of a guard employed at the Kingston penitentiary who was killed in 1926. Under the same authority in 1927 his widow was granted an allowance of $600 per annum. That amount has not been increased.

Before I give the floor to the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean, who assures me his remarks will be brief, I should like to place on the record my concurrence in the remarks made by the Minister of Justice regarding the point of order. Therefore, I

should ask the hon. member to give his cooperation to the Chair, in the light of my concurrence in those remarks, by confining himself to a consideration of the estimates of this department as nearly as he possibly can.

I will be very brief, Mr. Chairman. You have not given your ruling on the point of order. I was directing my remarks toward having this matter brought under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice instead of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. At the bottom of page 4487 of Hansard I had this to say in French:
(Translation):
I quote the Hon. W. Monteith, Minister of National Health and Welfare:
Mr. Speaker, I have been investigating this situation for some months in co-operation with my colleague, the Minister of Justice.
(Text):
Therefore, it was being studied by both departments. If I cannot bring the matter up now I do not know when I shall be able to bring it up. This seems to nje to be the proper time. I still believe I was in order until an hon. member across the chamber asked me the question, what are goof balls? He will find the answer at page 8 of the translation section of Hansard of May 25, 1961. The definition is given there.
Before I take my seat I should like to say that I sympathize with the Minister of Justice. I realize he is going to have a very difficult problem to handle because he will have to stop the sale of certain drugs. This may bring about a hardship on certain classes of society but since we are faced with a problem which must be dealt with we cannot delay and let it go on any longer. Therefore, I ask the minister whether he will not give this matter every possible consideration so that the proper measures will be taken to protect our youth in the future and goof balls not be available to them at any time.

The remarks of the Minister of Justice having to do with the implementation of legal justice are commendable. As I understood him, he obtains the services of the most competent lawyers in order to see that cases handled by the crown are handled in the best possible way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Within the requirements of the case. I did not mean to say that we always go to the man at the very top of the profession because that is not necessary in every case we have.

I understood the minister to say the most competent, I accepted that as meaning that the department selected a competent person. That is the sense in which

I am accepting it. So far as prosecutions under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act are concerned, it seems that the most competent lawyers or firms of lawyers are Conservatives. This may be coincidental. Before the committee took recess at one o'clock I had raised a question regarding the relationship between a Mr. Whitfield and the Canadian Marconi Company as it was affected by the bills of rights. In replying at that time the minister proceeded to draw what he called a logical conclusion from my remarks, and then proceeded to say that it was the advancement of an idea leading to dictatorship in granting arbitrary powers to the minister. Of course, this is not what I was suggesting at all. Further, I would say that when it comes to this government introducing legislation in this house, albeit prior to the time that the bill of rights was introduced, which is contrary to the bill of rights and which in fact places dictatorial powers in the hands of certain individuals and which in fact eliminates in one sense the operation of the courts as an integral part of our legal processes, hon. members will find this in the Feeds Act, being chapter 14 of the 1960 statutes. I merely bring this instance to the attention of the committee because this act contains sections which grossly violate the bill of rights and which, in my opinion, should be dealt with in somewhat the same manner as the Fisheries Act was dealt with. In other words, there should be a revision of this act to repeal those particular sections so that the bill of rights may really mean something.
Section 8 of the Feeds Act, Mr. Chairman, gives authority to an inspector to seize articles by means of or in relation to which he reasonably believes that a violation has been committed either against the act or the regulations. This is an arbitrary power, a dictatorial authority given to an inspector appointed under the Feeds Act to deprive an individual, contrary to the bill of rights, of his right to property and without due process of law. Presumably the word "reasonable" refers to reasonable grounds in the mind of the inspector, who reasonably believes that the Feeds Act or the regulations have been violated.
In addition, he reasonably believes that the property so confiscated or so seized was used to commit the offence. The act further provides that the inspector may release this property after a period of six months if a charge has not been laid. Here we find authority given by this government, and endorsed by this parliament, to a civil servant to deprive a person of property contrary to the bill of rights, and completely at variance with the minister's statement relating to the growing need to have the courts function as an integral part of our judicial system. The act further provides that if litigation is entered

into the goods so seized may be forfeited to the crown in addition to any other sort of fine or penalty imposed by the courts if the individual is found guilty.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that it is not in keeping with our good sense in attempting to discuss these things on an impartial basis for the minister to draw logical conclusions from the remarks of one member, and then extend those logical conclusions to include a charge of advancing a dictatorial type of system. I think those remarks are completely unfair, unjustified and are not what the minister, upon reflection, would call logical conclusions. In any event, even if he does consider they are logical conclusions, then we must come to another logical conclusion, namely, that this government does believe there are cases in which it is permissible to have the bill of rights violated by a statute of this parliament, a statute which was introduced by a colleague of the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Agriculture. The Feeds Act introduced by this government does violate the bill of rights in that it permits an individual to be deprived of property without due process of law, unless one extends the term "due process of law" to include dictatorial powers given by statute to an inspector. The act permits the minister to deprive an individual of his property for a period of six months without even getting around to laying a charge, and then to give that property back. The property may be of a perishable nature. It may be grain or it may be property which the farmer, for the sake of argument, needs in the conduct of his particular business, such as a truck or motor vehicle or some farm implement that he cannot use and which depreciates with the passage of time. I feel that this act also, to some extent, deprives an individual of the right to a fair hearing.
Another section of the Feeds Act provides that in a criminal prosecution-this is section 10 (2),-it is merely sufficient for the crown to prove the offence was committed by an employee or agent of the person accused, whether or not the employee or agent is identified or whether or not the employee or agent is actually prosecuted for the offence. In this instance we are talking about a function of the Attorney General of Canada, and we have finally found a case in which he is obligated to take some action. In this case the individual charged is being deprived of the right to a fair hearing because he has not had the opportunity of confronting the employee or agent or witness against him, nor has he had the opportunity to crossexamine the witness against him.
In this case we have action on the part of the government in introducing a bill, endorsed

by the cabinet, at exactly the same time as the cabinet was considering and endorsing the bill of rights at the last session and which is indicative of an effort on the part of the government to operate in two different ways. On the one hand, the government is trying to say we will have a bill of rights that will protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of the individual; we will have a bill of rights which will say an individual shall not be deprived of his property except by due process of law; we will have a bill of rights which will say an individual is entitled to a fair hearing. Then, on the other hand, the government introduces a piece of legislation like the Feeds Act which in these two instances-there are about 10 others to which I shall not refer-violates these principles of the bill of rights about which this government gloats so much.
I think, Mr. Chairman, when we have the state of affairs where the minister is coming to some logical conclusion, as he calls it, and then founding on that conclusion a presumption of a dictatorial situation while at the same time the minister and his colleagues are guilty of violating the bill of rights itself, it is a rather sad situation. The government has violated the bill of rights, first, by enacting this Feeds Act; second, by retaining on the statute books, without amendment, other legislation such as the Customs Act and the Income Tax Act, which are in conflict with this bill of rights. In so far as the Income Tax Act is concerned this is not my opinion alone because there is a court decision, I believe in the province of Quebec, supporting this point of view.
I think it is a sad and sorry state of affairs, Mr. Chairman, when we have a minister with the intellect and ability of this minister, as was evidenced by the article written by Mr. Nicholson to which the hon. member for Port Arthur referred, lauding to the high heavens the efficacy of the bill of rights and how much it means, a minister who belongs to a political party which is shipping out propaganda prepared by Allister Grosart to the effect that the bill of rights really means something in this country, while at the same time drafting legislation which contravenes the bill of rights and is completely contradictory to it. This government, at the same time, refuses to introduce amendments to such legislation as the Income Tax Act and the Customs Act, both of which contain provisions that contravene the bill of rights in a terrible way.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, when we have a minister who belongs to a government that has this sort of record of supporting legislation which is contradictory to the bill of rights, supporting legislation which permits

individuals to be deprived of their property, supporting legislation which really removes the courts of this nation from their position as an integral part of the judicial system, we must look askance at any spurious reasoning on the part of that minister or his government in coming to so called logical conclusions on the basis of opinions expressed by other hon. members.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I answer this at once because this is the second year in which my hon. friend and others in his group have made similar assertions with regard to the Feeds Act, all of which are equally unfounded, and it is time they were answered again at once.
My hon. friend makes the assertion, and appears to believe that it will gather strength by repetition because he repeated it many times, that the Feeds Act is directly contrary to the bill of rights. The fact of the matter is that the Feeds Act is not contrary to the bill of rights and does not contravene it in any particular in letter or in spirit. Of course we had the bill of rights in mind in 1960 when the Feeds Act and other statutes of that year were drafted and were presented to the house. We took care, as we have taken care ever since 1957, that no statute that we present to the House of Commons will be contrary to the bill of rights because that was one of the basic views of this government as it still is.
My hon. friend refers to section 8 of the bill which gives an inspector the right to seize property which he believes has been used to commit a violation of the act. There is seizure, yes; and there is nothing contrary to the bill of rights in authorizing seizure of property which is believed on reasonable grounds to have been used for the commission of an offence against our laws, but there is no forfeiture without due process of law.
The very section to which my hon. friend refers goes on in its succeeding words to provide that the property shall be restored to the person from whom it was seized, at the end of six months unless within that time judicial proceedings have been instituted in respect of the violation. Then it goes on to provide that it is only as a result of conviction for the offence that the property may be retained by the crown: it is only then that the owner may be deprived of his property. That scheme was developed with the bill of rights very much in mind.
This committee will be aware of the fact that in many statutes in the past providing for seizure, the seizure became forfeiture, in many cases without due process of law, without the owner, whether innocent or otherwise, having any chance to assert his 90205-6-343
Supply-Justice
innocence of the crime or offence in connection with which the goods were seized. Whether innocent or otherwise, he was deprived of his property rights without the necessity of any conviction.
Here, because of our awareness of the bill of rights and the principle upon which legislation of this kind should in our view be founded, we have deliberately provided that there would be no forfeiture except on conviction and then the court may order the goods forfeited. Nothing then can be clearer than that forfeiture-that is actual deprivation of property-can only come about by due process of law. And in order to make certain that the crown cannot in effect deprive a person of his property simply by seizing it and then refraining from bringing action on the offence, it is provided that unless proceedings are started within six months the goods must be restored. That provision again was put in out of an abundance of caution. We do not believe that responsible administrators would be likely to follow such a course, but it is possible that they might do so. We therefore put in that provision expressly to make it impossible for the crown effectively to deprive a person of the enjoyment or ownership of property by seizing it and then just leaving the matter in abeyance. Hence there is no contravention of the bill of rights there. Indeed, the section was clearly drafted with the principle of the bill of rights very much in mind.
The other point that my hon. friend makes is that the bill contains a provision that makes it clear that although an offence may have been committed by an employee, it is sufficient to prove or to establish that it was committed by that employee or agent of the accused without the necessity of identifying personally who that employee or agent was and that then the owner is liable for the offence.
It is a well understood principle of criminal law, as it has been for years, and indeed it is a well understood principle of common law -and it is not contrary to the bill of rights -employers are liable for the acts of their employees committed in the course of their employment. The criminal liability of an employer for the act of his employee committed in the course of his duties is a matter that has been well understood and well recognized and that the bill of rights does not in any way challenge. But it must be borne in mind that even although that is a fairly complete liability, the Feeds Act does not relieve the crown of any onus of proof with respect to the offence. The crown must prove that the offence was committed by an employee of a person charged. They do not have

to prove by name who that individual was but they would have to prove that it was an employee or agent of the person charged. They cannot just come along and say "We know that somebody committed this offence and we think it was an employee of the person charged". They have to prove that it was an employee or agent of the person charged. Then the well known doctrine of liability for the acts of employees or agents authorized and committed in the course of their employment speaks for the rest of the situation.
I am sorry if my hon. friend does not, as I expect he will not, accept my explanation. However, I can only assure him that all the persons with whom I have discussed this act and in whose advice as experts I have confidence, have assured me that technically it has been drawn with the bill of rights concept in mind and that there is nothing in the act which in any sense runs counter to the bill of rights. This is the technical situation, and it is the same with regard to the spirit and intent of that act. As I have indicated, because of our awareness of the bill of rights and the bill of rights concept and the principle upon which we believe legislation should be founded, even though the bill of rights had not been enacted we carried its spirit into the Feeds Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman should not try to put the blame on me when he is convicted out of his own mouth. I am not going to carry this argument further. It will be obvious to any hon. member who is prepared to look at this matter dispassionately, on which side of this discussion reason is to be found, though I know it will not be admitted by the hon. member who has just spoken. There is a further misunderstanding which will be obvious, I suggest, to everyone, though, once again, I do not think for a moment it will be admitted by the hon. member for Skeena. The hon. member persists in saying that it is a mistake to give the Minister of Justice responsibility for determining whether or not a statute is contrary to the provisions of the bill of rights. I point out for the information of the committee that the bill of rights does not give the minister any such responsibility. The courts, and the courts alone will determine

whether a statute is contrary to the provisions of the bill of rights. I endeavoured to explain this in the course of the debate on the bill of rights.
It is true there is an obligation imposed on the minister to report to the House of Commons whether there is in his opinion anything inconsistent between a particular bill and the provisions of the bill of rights. This is the one occasion on which, as far as I know, the minister has a statutory duty to advise the House of Commons. But the House of Commons does not have to accept his advice. The house can say, if it wishes, tha it does not agree, and may take the view that a particular bill is contrary to the provisions of the bill of rights, notwithstanding the report made by the Minister of Justice. The House of Commons is the master of its own decisions, and the Minister of Justice neither can nor wishes to dictate to it. But whether the minister is right or wrong, and whether the House of Commons accepts his opinion or not, it is the courts and the courts alone which have to make the final decision, and this was the system envisaged in the bill of rights, as we endeavoured to make clear at the time.
As far as all the other red herrings trailed by the hon. member for Skeena are concerned, may I say to him again that it is perfectly clear I am not in the least embarrassed by any report I may have to make. I did not report on one particular bill because I did not think it was properly before the house, but I stated without hesitation, when the proper occasion arose, that in my view the Fisheries Act as it previously existed contained provisions contrary to what is contained in the bill of rights, and this government introduced legislation to remove those provisions and bring the act into conformity with the bill of rights. The hon. member will find another bill to be introduced shortly where provision is made for bringing a statute into conformity with the bill of rights by amending an existing statute. We have no embarrassment about saying that a measure is contrary to the provisions of the bill of rights and taking action to amend it when we present bills to the house. However, with deference to the views of others, I must be allowed to interpret for myself what my duty is and I suggest I can scarcely be criticized if I interpret my responsibility as being not to make a report to the house at the wrong time.

The minister says he does not expect me to be in accord with the views he has expressed. Technically speaking, it is true that the courts interpret our statutes and find out what they mean, but in the first instance the minister has a duty to examine

bills and say whether or not they are consistent with the provision of the bill of rights. He is ordered to examine every bill presented to the House of Commons with that purpose in mind. Certainly this involves interpreting those statutes in the light of the requirements of the bill of rights. It is in this sense that I used that expression. I do not think the minister would deny that he has the obligation to examine bills from this point of view. Certainly, when they become statutes the courts are involved and would then determine whether or not they are consistent with the provisions of the bill of rights, along the same lines as the decision with respect to the Income Tax Act in Quebec and the decision reached in the community of Lillooet in British Columbia concerning whether a certain section of the Indian Act is in conflict with the bill of rights. However, the minister has the initial responsibility of reviewing new legislation and it is in this sense that I say it is a mistake to give this authority to a political figure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:

That does not represent my view of the situation, and I would suggest it should not be the view of the committee generally. Any discussion in regard to the application of section 3 of the bill of rights is, of course, in order. However, I suggest that in any discussion based on the provisions of any act, one should not confuse the responsibilities of the minister, the government, or parliament itself. It is for that reason I have expressed some doubt as

to the propriety of many of the comments which have been made since I returned to this chamber this afternoon. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I will now pass to another subject which will probably put the discussion on more solid ground.
The minister announced the introduction of:
A bill to carry out a narcotics control program, a bill to revise the Criminal Code to deal with dangerous sexual offenders and matters of that sort and also a bill to amend the Food and Drugs Act to deal with barbiturates.
The point I wish to make is that penalties are not proportionate to the crimes committed.
I see that section 138 of the Criminal Code authorizes judges to sentence to life imprisonment or to whipping, according to the judgment of the one who hears the case, any man who is found guilty of having had sexual intercourse with a woman, other than his wife, who is less that 14 years old, regardless of whether the accused knew or did not know that his victim was less that 14. Judges are not compelled to pass such sentence; they merely have the authority of doing so.
I feel that when a child under 12 is raped, the minimum sentence should be made more strict.
We have heard of psychopaths attacking chidren four or five years old and causing such harm to them that the latter were practically maimed for life, not to mention the dangerous inclination they were given by coming into contact too early with things they should have learned much later in life.
Yet, some judges, either because they lack firmness or for some other reason, have handed out sentences of only three to four years while the victim was left to suffer all her life from the attack. Minimum sentences should be more stringent in such cases.
Since the minister is presently preparing a bill in that regard I think he should provide for a stiffer minimum sentence and take away from the judges the authority of passing a lighter sentence, at their discretion.
Supply-J ustice
When the victim is a child of less than 12, when violence is involved, when the victim's personality has been practically destroyed, not only should the penalty be life imprisonment but there should be a minimum of 25 years detention with the whip as an extra.
Perhaps it will be said that I am a sadist. Yesterday evening, I heard a psychiatrist say on television that those who demand the retention of capital punishment are sadists, in a way. Such sadism is good for the protection of society. Our first concern should be the protection of society rather than the protection of criminals.
This is why I suggest that the sentence should be at least 25 years when a child is violently assaulted to the extent that it will be marked for the rest of its life.
I suggest that in such cases the minimum sentence be 25 years in the penitentiary with flogging.
A judge should be empowered to impose capital punishment to an individual convicted of such a crime. Capital punishment applies to kidnapping in the United States, and the individual convicted of that crime goes to the electric chair.
For my part, I think rape involving a child is a far more odious crime and, therefore, I do not think that 25 years with flogging is too much. I even suggest that the judge be allowed to sentence the convict to capital punishment under certain circumstances.
Mr. Chairman, I now turn to another field, narcotics.
There are those who will say that the narcotics act is the responsibility of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
However, it must be remembered that the Minister of National Health and Welfare cannot amend the narcotics act without first consulting the Department of Justice.
And as the minister indicated yesterday, a new bill will be submitted shortly. Under the circumstances, and following the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), I say we must make every effort to try to cure the drug addicts.
I think very severe penalties should be imposed when it is proven that a person was the leader of a narcotic ring, as happened recently in Montreal.
Indeed, I consider the drug distributor as guilty of an even greater offence than murder, because he kills the personality and draws the victim of this vice into a dead end.

Supply-J ustice
Such a person should get not ten years, as it happened, but a minimum of 25 years and the lash.
Furthermore, in such a case, the judge should be entitled to impose the death sentence, because the drug peddler has killed the souls of people by destroying their personality. Those victims may later become murderers and be sent to the gallows.
A person who organizes the sale of narcotics in this country, thus promoting a new attitude on the part of drug addicts, is worse than a murderer.
In that case, the only true murderer is probably not the one who killed, but the one who prepared him for it by supplying the necessary drugs and inciting him to commit the offence.
That is why I ask the Minister of Justice, to see to it, when drafting those laws that we shall discuss, that they at least be strict enough to be a deterrent for those pushers who accumulated millions by selling the drugs. For, having been sentenced to ten years' imprisonment, they will probably be released after five, and return to society to enjoy their accrued capital under the very noses of their victims. The matter is important, and I shall ask the minister to study very seriously that aspect of the legislation in order to protect society not so much against the murderer, who committed the act because of the drugs sold to him, and therefore tends to be considered as the real offender, but against the narcotics pusher who is the true offender. Society must be protected against those swindlers at any price.
I therefore ask the minister to provide stricter legislation with regard to such people, rather than murderers, because the latter are in a way, often the victims of individuals who, all their lives have made profit out of vice.

Mr. Pallet!: If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this matter because I think there may be something to be added to what has already been said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond and the hon. member for Skeena. They have very carefully referred to Beauchesne, paragraphs 380, 385 and 87. However, the matter hinges on the interpretation of standing order 19 (1) and (2). If I may, I should like to refer for a moment to some of the documents of the house itself in order to assist Your Honour in interpreting this particular section.
I think the matter is one of considerable importance to the private members of this house. The time allocated to them is set out on definite hours or definite days. If for 90205-6-344i
Private Bills
some reason or another-and I am not suggesting that this was the situation in this case-an hon. member's bill is not reached until the private members hour is fairly well along, it is not beyond the realm of possibility that a point of order should be raised by that member with, for example, even 15 minutes to go of the hour and that such time could be used up in that way. It is not a question of a few minutes-I just used that figure by way of illustration-but it is a question of whether this procedure might not be used as a device some time in the future for the purpose of getting an hon. member's bill in a priority position on the order paper or by way of a device to maintain it there.
With that point in mind, I think this decision is probably one of the most serious ones affecting the private members of the house that Your Honour has been called upon to make for some time. Standing order 19 states:
(1)	Questions put by members and notices of motions, not taken up when called may (upon the request of the government) be allowed to stand and retain their precedence: otherwise they will disappear from the order paper. They may, however, be renewed.
(2)	Orders not proceeded with when called, upon the like request,-
And it has been ruled by Your Honour in this house that "upon the like request" refers to a request of the government.
-may be allowed to stand retaining their precedence; otherwise they shall be dropped and be placed on the order paper for the next sitting after those of the same class at a similar stage.
(3)	All orders not disposed of at the adjournment of the house shall be postponed until the next sitting day, without a motion to that effect.
In ruling I think Your Honour must determine what is meant by the words "proceeded with when called". I would refer Your Honour to the record of this house which is called Votes and Proceedings. Nowhere in it in reference to orders do you find a question called. I refer to the day on which this particular matter was dealt with, namely Friday, May 19. Proceeding to some bills that preceded Bill No. C-30, we find in Votes and Proceedings of May 19, at page 565, under the heading "Public Bills" and referring to Bill No. C-27:
The order being read for the second reading of Bill C-27, an act to amend the the Senate and House of Commons Act (Solicitor General's Eligibility);
Then we go on to the next one and we find the following:
The order being read for the second reading of Bill C-29, an act to amend the Representation Act;
Following this recital in Votes and Proceedings we then have the recital that the hon. member made a motion, duly seconded, in the particular cases. I suggest to Your Honour

Private Bills
that under standing order 19 (1) and (2) the motion being "called" is identical with being "read"; and so in Votes and Proceedings also of May 19 with respect to the bill in question, namely Bill No. C-30, we find the following:
The order being read for the second reading of Bill C-30, an act to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act:
I submit, Your Honour, that this is the same as being called under standing order 19. Whether or not the point of order raised was a bona fide or a bogus one is a matter I think Your Honour is not called upon to decide. I think it is a question of these particular words.
In the event that "called" is not the same as "read", some steps will have to be taken to rewrite Votes and Proceedings for many years, because it is in this context that the official records of the house have been kept.
If "read" is the same as "called", the authorities referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway contained in Beau-chesne, citations 380, 385 and 87, are pertinent. Your Honour will also find in May, fifteenth edition, and all other authorities, that when an order is read-he refers to "read" and not "called"-and not proceeded with, it is dropped.
I submit these points for Your Honour's consideration in making this very vital decision, which is one that could have very far reaching effects on the rights of hon. members of this house to proceed with the business that is "called" by our wording but "read" by the wording in the official record of proceedings of the house and by the wording in the authorities for other houses.
For these reasons I submit that the arguments advanced by the hon. members for Vancouver-Kingsway and Vancouver-Bur-rard are most important and certainly should be given very earnest and serious consideration by Your Honour.

Mr. Speaker, I consider this matter to be of such importance that the house should give serious attention to it, because the ruling Your Honour will make will stand as a precedent for a very considerable time, if not forever. We are faced here with a suggested reversal of long established practice.
The hon. members who have preceded me have read our own rule in the house. They have quoted from Beauchesne. I should like to refer to the other references so that we have on record a clear picture of what has been the practice of the house, the rules and the comments on the rules over the years with regard to dropped motions or dropped orders.
Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, page 221, contains very much the same wording that we have in our rule. The complete citation is page 221, section XII, subsection 2 of rule 32 of that day, and it reads:
Orders not proceeded with when called, upon the like request, may be allowed to stand retaining their precedence; otherwise they shall be dropped and be placed on the order paper for the next sitting after those of the same class at a similar stage.
Obviously, sir, this has been the long established practice of the House of Commons because the third edition of Beauchesne dates back to 1903 and I suppose the fourth edition is a repetition of that.
I should also like to draw Your Honour's attention to the reference in Beauchesne, fourth edition, page 81 which was read by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne); but there is an additional sentence there which is interesting. The hon. member read as follows, and this is page 81, citation 87, subsection 4:
It is one of the fundamental principles of parliamentary procedure that when nothing is done respecting an order of business it is struck out and cannot make further progress until the procedure regulating its passage has been regulated by the house.
I suggest, sir, that this order of business having been called, or read out, and nothing having been done with it, according to our rules and the practice of the house it was then automatically struck out. Beauchesne goes on to say:
Neither the Speaker nor any officer of the house have the power to move it forward.

I suggest, sir, that this order should have been struck out, dropped entirely or placed at the bottom of the list. Then the onus would have been on the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) to draw to Your Honour's attention whether or not that was established practice and whether it should have been dropped. But no officer of the house should have placed on the order paper in the position in which it appears, an order that had been read out and which had not been proceeded with. It should have been struck out or dropped, and it seems to me that the action taken exceeded the authority which is permitted according to the sentence which I have read from Beauchesne.
Then, in times of doubt concerning matters of rules and procedure we look to May, and the sixteenth edition of May at page 392 has a further comment to make with regard to dropped orders and indicates, of course, that they may be revived. May I point out in passing that although we suggested this order should have been dropped or placed at the bottom of the list, this does not mean further discussion on it is prohibited at a later date; it is not being thrown out entirely, because it can be revived by the hon. member. There is no prohibition involved in this at all. It is just a question of the order of precedence. May, at page 392, has this to say:
When an order of the day has been read, the proceedings thereon may be cut short by the adjournment of the house whilst those proceedings are in course of transaction. An order of the day, in such cases, or if, when the order is read, no day is appointed for its future consideration, drops off the notice paper, as the house has made no order thereon.
I suggest to you, sir, that the house was unable to take any action with regard to second reading of Bill No. C-30 because of the intervention of the proposer of the bill, at his own desire, in order, as we see it, to prevent consideration of the measure. According to the rules we have quoted to you and the citations we have placed on record in Hansard this particular order should not now be standing at the head of the order paper. The opportunity was available for the proposer to move it. He did not take that opportunity. Therefore, the house took no action with regard to it and the order is a dropped order and should not stand where it now stands.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUGGESTED REVISION OP MEDIATION AND CONCILIATION PROCESSES
speechtext:
The question before the Chair is one of considerable interest and importance and one to which I have given a good deal of thought in the interval since it was raised. I think certain principles are clear enough but I have one difficulty which I have not been able to resolve, and perhaps if I set out my views on the position of the

Private Bills
order for second reading of Bill No. C-30 I may be able to get some assistance on that doubtful point.
When an order such as this order of the house for a second reading of a bill is read by the Clerk, as was done in this case, the matter is not before the house for discussion until the motion has been moved. The motion must be taken up. After the order is read, various things may happen and most of the contingencies are provided for in our standing order No. 19. If the order is not proceeded with it is dropped under paragraph 2 of standing order 19 and it is argued that that is the applicable clause in the circumstances we now have under consideration. If the order is not disposed of, then paragraph 3 applies, and paragraph 3 of standing order 19 says:
All orders not disposed of at the adjournment of the house shall be postponed until the next sitting day, without a motion to that effect.
In fact, this matter was not disposed of- whether rightly or wrongly is a matter still to be determined. But if hon. members will turn to Hansard for the report of the debate in question the facts will be clear enough. The order was read by the clerk assistant, and the hon. member in whose name the order stood was then given the floor for the purpose of moving his motion. A motion can be put before the house either by being read from the chair, which is the customary practice- I suppose, to save time-or it can be moved by the hon. member in whose name it stands before it is read from the chair. The hon. member was given the floor for that purpose. I do not need to repeat what transpired, because it is set out in full at page 5083. The hon. member first suggested that it was six o'clock. It was not, in fact, six o'clock and the house did not concur in his request that it be called six o'clock. Then, without apparently relinquishing the floor or without any intervening action, he said, "Then I should like to raise a point of order".
It has been argued, and I think, correctly by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale) that a member should not rise on a point of order in order to deter or impede the progress of his own motion. In other words, he cannot raise a point of order against himself. I think that is a sound principle. It is certainly sound in forensic practice-a man cannot both approbate and reprobate if he is moving a motion. He cannot say, at the same time: "I am out of order in moving, but I move." That is what the hon. member, in effect, did. I accept that argument-the argument that it is not open to a member of the house who has the floor for the purpose of moving a motion or carrying on some proceeding in his name, or making a speech,

to make a point of order against his own progress in that manner. Having got thus far, I am up against the difficulty that, in fact, the hon. member's point of order was entertained instead of being rejected at that time, as I suggest it could have been rejected. And it was being entertained when the sitting came to a conclusion at six o'clock. Therefore, the question which is unresolved by the argument so far is this: assuming that what has been said is correct and that the duty of the hon. members was either to decline to proceed, or to proceed, or to move the postponement, or to take whatever other course was open to him, what is the position when as I have said he took a course which was not open to him, to raise a point of order against himself? As I have said, the hon. member did in fact proceed to speak without a motion having been made. He was heard, and six o'clock intervened. That is the way the order paper stood when the clerks had the duty of preparing the order paper for the next day. If the point had been taken at the time when the hon. member for Skeena had the floor for the sole purpose of moving his motion or asking that it should stand, and for no other purpose, then this difficulty about the subsequent order paper would not have arisen. Or, if the time had been sufficient for the nature of the point of order, which, appears to have no substance, to have been determined, it would then have been necessary to move second reading, and the hon. member would then have been under the obligation of moving, or allowing his motion to drop.
However, time intervened while this irregular discussion was proceeding and the question now is whether that intervention of time saves the place of this motion on the order paper. That is the difficult point which is involved; whether the point of order, having been in fact entertained, and the time having lapsed, allows the hon. member to escape the consequences of the irregularity of his course. In fact the order was read, but had not been disposed of, and subsection 3 of standing order 19 states positively that all orders not disposed of at the adjournment of the house, shall be postponed to the next sitting day without a motion to that effect. Should I interfere with the order as it stands today on the order paper? To do so I should have to cancel all that which was done on the last day, and I do not think hon. members would expect me to take that course.
I should like to present one other point of view before disposing of the matter, and then ask for the opinions of hon. members regarding the difficulty involved.
I am satisfied that when an order is read, it is not before the house, until the motion

has been moved. Beauchesne says, in citation No. 380, to which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) referred, that when a bill comes up for second reading in its proper course, and one of the clerks at the table reads the order aloud, the member in charge of the measure will then move its second reading. I accept that as a correct statement of normal practice. Similarly, I accept as a statement of normal practice that which is contained in citation 385;
If, when the order of the day is read at the table, no motion be made for the second reading, or other stage of the bill, or for its postponement, it becomes a dropped order.
However, I point this situation out for hon. members' consideration: After an order is read there may be an intervening procedure before a motion is made. It is within the rights of any member of the house, other than the member whose duty it is to move the motion, to raise a point of order. For instance, the point of order which we are considering now could well be taken after the reading of an order but before the consequent motion; in other words, the point that the order of the day is not properly on the order paper. The point of order arises as soon as the order is read, and before the motion is proceeded with.
As another instance, a point of order might well be taken under standing order 74, that the bill was not printed in both English and French and therefore could not yet be read the second time. This point of order could well be taken after the Clerk had read the order at the table, but before the motion had been put. If such a point of order was taken, it would then have to be discussed. The discussion would then have intervened and prolonged the time during which the mover of the second reading of the bill must move his motion, or decide not to proceed with it. In fact, that is what did happen in respect of this particular bill, C-30. I have said it could happen, and it did happen.
The difficulty involved is, that what did intervene was something which should not have been allowed to intervene. It having been allowed to intervene, I do not intend unless hon. members can persuade me otherwise, to alter the effect of the rule as contained in subsection 3 of standing order 19 which would allow the order to keep its place on the order paper.
If any hon. member has any suggestion to contribute to this aspect of the problem, with which I am faced, and before I dispose of the matter, I should like to hear him.

Mr. Speaker, it is a maxim of equity that he who
Private Bills
seeks justice must do justice. I suggest that has a pertinent effect in respect of this particular point, because the point of order is a bogus one, and was raised by the hon. member who was called upon to move the particular bill. The meaning of that maxim surely must be that if a person wishes to rely on the rules, in order to advance his cause, he must, in the terms of that phrase, do justice himself. The corollary of that is that he is estopped from relying on the technicality of a point of order if he raises the point of order himself.
In regard to the question as to whether the point of order had been entertained, I do not think the house can properly be seized with a bogus point of order, particularly one raised by the hon. member who was moving the motion. I suggest, therefore, that the point of order which was raised has no effect at all, and the situation is simply as though the passage of time had lapsed, and it was not possible for the Speaker in the time that intervened to make a ruling in respect of it.
Your Honour mentioned another course during your remarks, as to whether any hon. member had objected to the member raising this point of order. It will be noted that at page 5083 of Hansard for May 19, 1961 it is recorded right after the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) said "Then I should like to raise a point of order," that an hon. member said "The order has been called". I suggest, in view of that, it was impossible or improper for the hon. member for Skeens to raise a point of order against himself.
Returning again to the original point-he who seeks justice must do justice-I suggest in procedural terms, this means that if one seeks to rely on the procedures of this house, or of the courts, one must not offend those procedures one seeks to invoke to support his cause. I suggest that is exactly what the hon. member has sought to do by talking out, in effect, his own bill.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make two brief comments. First of all, when the hon. member for Skeena rose to the point of order, it would have been impossible for any other member to rise on another point of order, because he would not be recognized. I suggest, therefore, this is the first opportunity we have had to do so.
The second point I should like to mention is that the hon. member for Skeena referred to the procedure followed on April 21 in respect to Bill No. C-20 amending the Small Loans Act. He suggested the procedure followed at that time was very similar to the present situation, in that when this bill was called for second reading the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) the mover of the

bill, said "Stand." The hon. member for As-siniboia, the leader of the party of which the hon. member for Skeena is a member, obviously had in mind very properly standing order 19 (2), which states that orders may be allowed to stand; but the point that is indicated very clearly-and the hon. member for Skeena gave this particular citation-is that the hon. member for Assiniboia realized that when the orders were called he had to take some sort of positive action. He had to request that the order be stood over, proceed with the motion for second reading or allow it to become a dropped order.
I suggest that by doing nothing the hon. member for Skeena has permitted his order to become a dropped order. The fact that he raised this point of order and that it was impossible for other members to intervene I suggest would have no effect on the ruling, Mr. Speaker. Your clear decision is to point out to the hon. member that he should have acted as soon as the order was called. Then, if he wished to raise a point of order, that was the time to do it. Since he chose to take no stand I would suggest that it became a dropped order, and that is the way it should stand now.
